newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Korean peace talks in doubt - U.S. envoy.
newsitem.headline: Korean peace talks in doubt - U.S. envoy.

text.p: North Korea could further delay a briefing in New York on proposed Korean peninsula peace talks, throwing into question the future of the four-nation peace negotiations, U.S. Ambassador James Laney said on Friday.

North Korea earlier this week delayed the briefing where details for the peace talks were to be thrashed out. The peace talks, including the United States, China and the two Koreas, were proposed by Washington and Seoul last April.
The briefing was originally set for Wednesday but Pyongyang, seeking a barter deal for 500,000 tonnes of grain with U.S. grain trader Cargill Inc, asked the meeting be delayed a week.

"Latest reports are that unless North Korea receives more grain or gets grain for the Cargill deal...they have no intention of going to the briefing," Laney told a news conference after a three-year assignment in Seoul.
"That puts a great deal of doubt on the four-party talks."

North Korea, following months of resistance, agreed in December to attend the crucial U.S.-South Korean briefing after negotiations with Washington that led to Pyongyang apologising for a September submarine incursion into the South.
The negotiations paved the way for Cargill Inc, the giant U.S. grain exporter, to receive a permit from Washington to barter grain for North Korean minerals.
The shipment is crucial for Pyongyang, which is suffering an acute food shortage after devastating floods in 1995 and 1996.
But Laney said no deal had yet been struck between Cargill and Pyongyang.
"As yet, Cargill has not found a sufficient basis for that barter. The United States government of course has nothing to do with private business," he said.
"So at this point it's a matter of North Korea and Cargill to work out an agreement."
During Laney's tenure in Seoul, U.S. contacts with North Korea grew significantly.

In 1994, Washington and Pyongyang signed a landmark nuclear deal to freeze and eventually dismantle North Korea's suspected nuclear arms programme in return for $4.5 billion in nuclear technology and interim energy supplies.
